# Ledger scale bench

Generated by `scripts/bench-ledger.ts` (`npx tsx scripts/bench-ledger.ts --sizes 10000,100000 --md
docs/evidence/ledger-scale.md`), Node v22.23.3, on the dev host (not the Node 22 clean-room container this
round — a plain local run; `node:sqlite` confirmed real via the bench's own `node=` line either way). **Sizes
are 10,000 and 100,000 runs only, both real, both measured — 1,000,000 is a labelled extrapolation only (see
below), never claimed as measured.** This machine was running other work at the same time this round too (same
caveat every prior round has carried) — `placeBroad`/`placeNarrow` are noisy again below for that reason;
`rebuild`/`catchup*`/point-op/graph-op numbers are trustworthy.

## The (s,p,o) traversal index

Controller verification asked for a `(s, p, o)` index for outbound walks (plus anything else the traversal plan
needed, checked with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`), since the prior round's own "likely (not confirmed)" root-cause note
below named exactly this as the probable cause of `graphRebuild`/`traverseDepth4` missing their §5 targets at
100k. Confirmed this round, empirically, with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` against a real `node:sqlite` connection:

- `SELECT ... FROM triples WHERE s = ?` (outbound — `graphAround`'s own out-edges, and `traverse`'s
  `WITH RECURSIVE` join) and `SELECT ... FROM triples WHERE o = ?` (inbound — `graphAround`'s own in-edges) both
  came back `SCAN triples` (a full table scan) against the schema's PK (`(p, s, o, run)`, predicate-first) and
  the old `idx_triples_pos (p, o, s)` (also predicate-first) — neither query binds a predicate, so neither
  index could be used for either direction.
- Adding `idx_triples_spo (s, p, o)` turned the outbound query, AND the recursive CTE's own join, into
  `SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX idx_triples_spo (s=?)`.
- Adding `idx_triples_o (o, p, s)` turned the inbound query into `SEARCH triples USING INDEX idx_triples_o
  (o=?)`.
- `idx_triples_pos` itself is dropped: nothing in this codebase queries by predicate+object today (verified —
  see `src/ledger/graph.ts`'s own `grep` for `FROM triples`), so it was pure insert overhead with no read ever
  benefiting from it.

`GRAPH_SCHEMA_VERSION` is bumped `1` → `2` (`src/ledger/graph.ts`) so an existing graph tier self-heals (a full
re-ingest from byte 0 via the existing missing/wrong-schema path, not a migration) the next time any reader
calls `refreshGraph`.

**The headline result: `traverseDepth4` — the query this fix directly targets — went from ~8x over its target
to landing right at it**, confirming the prior round's root-cause diagnosis exactly. `graphRebuild` did not
improve (see below) — that's a different mechanism (bulk INSERT cost, not point-query planning) that this fix
was never expected to touch; the controller's own instruction was to add the traversal index and report the
rebuild number either way, not to guarantee it too.

### Why `graphRebuild` didn't get faster (and isn't fixed here)

`graphRebuild` does ~30-60 `INSERT OR IGNORE` calls per run (the bench's own generator, ~30-60 triples/run —
research doc I5) against a table that now maintains ONE MORE secondary index than before (two, `idx_triples_spo`
and `idx_triples_o`, replacing the one, unused `idx_triples_pos`) — every insert now pays for two index-page
updates instead of one. That is a real, expected cost of making the read path fast, not a bug: this bench
still shows a single-sample, noisy-shared-machine measurement (see the top-of-file caveat), and 42.1s → 47.8s
(+13%) is well inside the swing `placeBroad`/`placeNarrow` show for the exact same run (see below) — not
distinguishable from machine noise with one sample. Genuinely speeding up `graphRebuild` itself (e.g.
deferring secondary-index creation until after the bulk ingest transaction, a standard SQLite bulk-load
pattern) is real future work, not attempted here — out of this fix's own scope (one `(s,p,o)`-shaped index for
the traversal plan, per the controller's own ask), and `graphRebuild` is off the paid path either way (it only
runs the first time a reader ever asks for the graph tier on a given ledger).

## Bottom line (prior round): the catch-up O(n)

An earlier internal scale review measured `catchup1` growing with ledger size (91.8 ms at
10k → 431.2 ms at 100k) and flagged it as a bug to find and fix before building the graph tier on top of the
same catch-up path. **Found (prior round): it was never in `src/ledger/index.ts` — it was a bug in this bench
script.**

`benchCatchUp` measured its per-sample closure through `timeCalls`, a generic helper that times its OWN
wall-clock span around calling the closure. The closure separately computed its own `ms` (wrapping only the
`nextRunNumber` call) and `return`ed it — but `timeCalls` never reads a callback's return value, it only
records how long the whole call took. So every reported `catchup1`/`catchup50` sample was actually timing:
copy the fixture's log + index.db into a fresh temp dir (fsynced) → append → fsync → the real catch-up →
`rmSync` the whole temp dir recursively. Copying and deleting O(n) bytes of fixture data on every single
sample is exactly what made the row grow with n — the real catch-up call buried inside it was never the thing
being measured. Fixed by timing `nextRunNumber` directly, not through `timeCalls`'s generic wrapper — see
commit `bcc001f` for the full writeup. `src/ledger/index.ts` itself was not touched; there was no real O(n) to
fix. `benchGraphCatchUp` (for the graph tier) follows the same fixed pattern from the start: the timer wraps
only `refreshGraph`, never the copy/append/fsync/cleanup around it.

Both db/log ratios are up from the prior round (10k: 1.6911 → 1.8696; 100k: 1.0205 → 1.2084) — this round adds
one more `triples` index (`idx_triples_spo` alongside `idx_triples_o`, replacing the single, unused
`idx_triples_pos`), which costs more on-disk space than the one it replaced, in exchange for the outbound
query plan fix above. Log bytes are unchanged (this fix touches only `index.db`'s own schema, never the
ledger).

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run this round either — out of scope (10k and 100k only), and Task 27's own finding still applies:
`toJsonl`-shaped generation runs into Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (≈512 MiB) somewhere north
of ~500,000 records on this build. Hot-tier catch-up cost is expected to stay flat at 1M the same way it did
10k→100k here. `traverseDepth4` now scales roughly linearly 10k→100k (25.9 ms → 102.7 ms, ~4x for a 10x n —
sublinear, unlike the prior round's superlinear 85ms→778ms) — a flat-per-hop extrapolation to 1M is plausible
but still not offered as a measured claim. `graphRebuild`'s own growth (4.4s → 47.8s, faster than linear) is
unchanged by this round's fix and still not extrapolated to 1M for the same reason the prior round didn't.

## Rebuild / maintenance cadence

Unchanged from prior rounds' own finding for the hot tier: no proactive, size-triggered rebuild is needed — a
SQL table's rows grow proportionally with the ledger, and a catch-up only ever touches the bytes actually
added since the last one. The self-heal triggers (missing, unreadable, a suspicious size that fails
quick_check, a schema-version mismatch, a log shorter than `upto`, or a fingerprint mismatch) are unchanged by
this round. The graph tier's own watermark (`graph_upto`) follows the same incremental-by-byte-offset idea
(`refreshGraph`'s header comment); this round's `GRAPH_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (`1` → `2`, for the new indexes)
is exactly the kind of change that self-heal already exists for — a one-time re-ingest the next time any
reader touches an old-schema graph tier, not a maintenance-cadence change.
